title: Exclusive: Inner-city workers at huge risk from AI
full_text:
Sydney's professional heartland is set to be reshaped by automation as hundreds of thousands of workers in the city's inner suburbs become more exposed to artificial intelligence-driven disruption than anywhere else in Australia.
More than 45 per cent of the tasks performed by employees in City of Sydney and North Sydney council areas are vulnerable to AI automation, new analysis shows.
Other local government areas where workplaces have high exposure include Ryde, which takes in the Macquarie Park jobs hub (43 per cent), Willoughby (42 per cent), and Parramatta (42 per cent).
Residents in Sydney's lower north shore and the eastern suburbs are also disproportionately vulnerable to AI disruption because of the high concentration of knowledge-economy jobs in those areas.
About 43 per cent of tasks performed by workers who live in North Sydney, Willoughby, Ku-ring-gai and Lane Cove councils are exposed to AI automation. That share is 42 per cent in the Woollahra and Waverley council areas.
This is a departure from previous waves of economic disruption, especially the automation and outsourcing of manufacturing activities in the 1980s and 1990s, which hit employment in outer suburbs and regional areas hardest.
The report by consultancy SGS Economics and Planning found city-based employees in finance, professional services, technology and business services are most likely to see their jobs change due to AI. Those workers and industries have been largely shielded from job displacements triggered by structural economic shifts in recent decades.
Alison Holloway, a partner at SGS Economics and Planning and the report's co-author, said the effects of AI automation would have a "different spatial pattern" to previous economic transitions caused by technological change.
"Earlier waves of automation took on routine, manual tasks, so their effects were felt most in manufacturing suburbs and farming regions," she said.
"AI can now take on parts of the cognitive work done in offices, and those jobs are concentrated in the professional heart of our cities."
The share of tasks vulnerable to AI automation declines with distance from Sydney's central business district - to around 40 per cent in the Hills Shire, 37 per cent in Blacktown council and 35 per cent in Hawkesbury council.
In parts of regional NSW, where a high share of work tasks require a physical presence, only about 30 per cent of work tasks are at risk of AI disruption.
Employment and Workplace Relations Minister Amanda Rishworth said there was no evidence of widespread AI-driven disruption to Australia's labour market.
"Workers need to have confidence that by adopting AI, they are not just training their own replacement," she said. "The Australian government is closely monitoring how AI affects jobs to ensure that workplace settings and supports for Australians impacted by changes in the labour market remain appropriate."
Rishworth said the Albanese government was promoting "safe AI adoption" in workplaces and that the AI Employment and Workplaces Forum, created this year, had brought together government, employers and unions to discuss AI's opportunities and challenges.
The report found work tasks performed in inner-city Melbourne had a high exposure to AI automation, especially the City of Melbourne (44.5 per cent) and Port Philip (42.3 per cent). Other urban areas with a relatively high share of work tasks vulnerable to AI automation include Adelaide City (43 per cent) City of Perth (43 per cent), the ACT (41 per cent) and Brisbane City (40 per cent).
For a century, automation has changed work on farms and in factories. During the past 30 years, the manufacturing sector's share of economic output has fallen steadily amid the introduction of industrial robots, reduced trade barriers and low-cost overseas competition.
Federal and state governments have provided a range of support programs to assist manufacturing firms and workers affected by this transition, which coincided with strong growth in knowledge-intensive services such as finance, professional services and information technology.
The SGS Economics and Planning report, released today, says the Australian economy "is transitioning again" as we enter an era where AI can perform an expanding range of tasks once reserved for highly skilled trades and professionals.
The analysis measured the exposure to AI automation of work tasks, not the probability of jobs disappearing altogether.
But Holloway said the disruptions caused by AI could require targeted programs to retrain employees and support for workers as they shift to different jobs.
"In the past, we've seen the closure of mines and things like car manufacturing, which has impacted whole communities, but this is now a different part of the economy and different locations that will be more affected," she said. "There is a lot we can learn from those previous transitions to think more strategically about what's coming with AI automation.
"It is a question of who benefits from these changes and who struggles."
A spokesperson for the NSW government said AI would bring "opportunities and changes" to the state's workforce.
"We established an Office of AI this year to help government monitor and respond to the impacts of this technology," the spokesperson said.
"Through the establishment of the Office of AI and ongoing investment in skills and training, we are working to navigate this technological change."
Jeremy Gill, head of policy at advocacy group the Committee for Sydney, said the city needed to prepare for the ways AI automation would change work patterns.
"This doesn't mean people living and working in areas at risk of high levels of AI automation will have their jobs replaced," he said.
"But it does mean the skills that they need, the kind of the tasks and the things they do in their jobs are going to change, and we need to make sure that they're ready for that and Sydney is ready for it."
Gill said assisting workers at the "beginning and the end of the work journey" would be crucial, especially education and skills development.
"New graduates entering the marketplace will be an important place to start; so we don't have generations entering the labour market that are not being prepared for it," he said.
"At the other end of the spectrum, how will we support workers for whom this might be very different technology, but they've still got 10 or 15 years left of work before they're able to retire?
"There is a risk that they could be left behind if they're not factored in and planned for."
Gill said many hands-on jobs in sectors like manufacturing, healthcare and construction were likely to prove more resilient to AI disruption.
"In Sydney, many of these jobs, and many of those who do them, are based in the west and southwest parts of the city," he said.
Council areas in regional NSW with a relatively high share of work tasks exposed to AI automation include Newcastle (38 per cent), Wollongong (37 per cent), Albury (37 per cent) and Armidale (37 per cent).
Holloway said policy measures might be required to ensure the economic benefits of AI adoption are effectively distributed.
"A big question is who benefits from that productivity uplift from AI? Does that go to private capital? Does that go to the owners of businesses, or does it actually benefit workers and those at the community level?" she said.
The SGS Economics and Planning analysis used estimates of how exposed each occupation is to AI automation made by federal agency Jobs and Skills Australia, along with census employment data, to map exposure both where people work and where they live.
